note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: sequence numbers match [0-9]{1,6} and are unique
clarifyingQuestions: Which request types exist besides REGISTER and FRIEND_REQUEST, and how are they formatted?
What is returned for each request: a status string, a list, or only some responses?
Can money move between users who are not friends?
What happens when a transfer would overdraw the sender?
Can a friend request be accepted twice?
hints: Each request touches at most two users: hash maps keyed by user name make every request O(1) after parsing.
Store pending friend requests by their sequence number so an accept request can find them directly.
Keep friendships as a set of ordered pair keys (smaller name first) and check balances before moving money.
invariants: the sum of all balances only changes on REGISTER
a pending request is consumed by at most one accept
friendship is symmetric
chooseWhen: Replaying an API log with per-entity state
tradeoffs: String parsing dominates; a stricter request schema would let the parser reject malformed lines
hack2hire:68e6bf5c605ab8e954684812.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: request log with registrations, friend requests, transfers between friends and balances

clarifyingQuestions: How long does refuelling take per liter?
Which dispenser does a driver pick when several are free?
What should be returned: the longest wait, total wait, or the per-car waits?
What happens when no dispenser can ever serve the front car?
hints: Fuel only decreases, so a car that no dispenser can serve now can never be served.
Cars start in queue order, so each start time is at least the previous one.
A car starts at the earliest free-at time among dispensers with enough fuel (but not before the previous car); pick the first such dispenser free then.
invariants: start times are non-decreasing in queue order
each dispenser serves one car at a time
chooseWhen: Queue simulations whose events can be computed directly instead of ticking a clock
tradeoffs: Event arithmetic is O(N) regardless of the amounts; a tick simulation is only feasible for tiny amounts
hack2hire:69c7f82d21f6ab4226966a80.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: three-dispenser queue, longest wait

constraints: each name has 2 to 5 words of [A-Za-z]{1,12}
clarifyingQuestions: How is the base username built from a full name?
Are middle names used?
How are duplicates disambiguated and how does that interact with the 8-character limit?
Can a numbered username collide with another person's base?
hints: Build the base once per name: first initial plus family name, lowercased, cut to 8 characters.
Duplicates need a suffix; shorten the base so base plus digits still fits in 8 characters.
Different bases can collide after truncation, so always test candidates against the set of issued names, and remember per base where the search stopped.
invariants: issued usernames are pairwise distinct
every username has length <= 8 and matches [a-z0-9]+
chooseWhen: Generating short unique identifiers from free-form names
tradeoffs: Per-base counters avoid rescanning suffixes but need extra memory per distinct base
hack2hire:699bb8776e73e4abccc9aa11.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: initial-plus-surname usernames with numeric suffixes

clarifyingQuestions: Are hours whole numbers, and is end the last moment the recipient is present?
Does every recipient need a gift, or do we maximise the number served?
Should the schedule itself be returned?
hints: Sweep the hours in order and decide who is served in each slot.
At each hour serve, among the recipients who are present, those whose availability ends soonest (exchange argument).
With only nine possible end hours, a counter per end hour replaces the heap.
invariants: a recipient is served at most once
no slot serves more than n recipients
chooseWhen: Unit-length jobs with release times, deadlines and parallel machines
tradeoffs: The bucket counter relies on the tiny hour range; general times need a real heap
hack2hire:67fda0b6d2adf72ba62b0ed9.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum deliveries with n parallel one-hour slots

clarifyingQuestions: Where does the player start, and which cell is the goal?
Is the answer reachability or the number of moves?
Can a step jump over obstacles?
What if the start cell is an obstacle?
hints: Every move costs one, so breadth-first search gives the fewest moves.
Parse a cell's directives into (direction, step) pairs; a missing number means 1.
Skip moves that leave the board or land on "X"; jumping over obstacles is allowed.
invariants: each cell is enqueued at most once
BFS distances never decrease along the queue
chooseWhen: Shortest paths with unit edge costs on implicit graphs
tradeoffs: Parsing lazily avoids work for unreachable cells but keeps the board strings alive
hack2hire:68c4834e97640ed3834dc7ca.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: fewest moves to the last cell

clarifyingQuestions: When several prefixes match, which one wins?
What is returned when no route matches?
Can the base address have bits set beyond the prefix length?
Can the same prefix appear twice?
hints: Convert dotted quads to 32-bit integers once.
A route with length k matches exactly when the top k bits agree: compare ip >> (32 - k) with the route network >> (32 - k).
Keep one map per length and probe lengths from 32 down; the first hit is the longest match.
invariants: each map holds only masked networks of its length
the first hit in descending length order is the longest match
chooseWhen: Longest-prefix lookups with few distinct prefix lengths
tradeoffs: A binary trie gives O(32) per query independent of the number of lengths but costs more memory per route
hack2hire:687eda22cdb08328ca5a8483.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest-prefix-match routing table

constraints: column names match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}, at most 10 per file
clarifyingQuestions: Is the header part of the output?
What if a key matches several processor rows?
Is the key column repeated in the output?
What happens to rows without a match?
Can values be empty, and do empty keys match?
hints: Find the key column index in each header first.
Index the processor rows by key in a hash map of lists so each customer row finds its matches directly.
Emit the combined header, then customer values plus processor values for every match.
invariants: output rows follow customer order, then processor order
every output row has the customer plus processor column count
chooseWhen: Equi-joins where one side fits in memory
tradeoffs: The hash index costs memory for the whole processor file; a sort-merge join would stream sorted inputs
hack2hire:6a1a0cc4c81f779dc6a2376b.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: inner join on one column

constraints: column names match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}, at most 10 per file

Is the key column repeated in the output?
What happens to rows without a match?
Can values be empty, and do empty keys match?

A customer row with no matches still produces one row.
Padding with m empty values is just m extra commas.

output rows follow customer order, then processor order

constraints: column names match [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}, at most 10 per file

Mark every processor row that was used.
Append the unused processor rows, each preceded by empty customer values.

constraints: each dependency list has 0 to 10 distinct ids
clarifyingQuestions: Can a task list prerequisites that do not exist yet?
What happens when a new task would create a cycle?
Which order is returned when several are valid?
Are tasks with missing prerequisites included?
hints: Adding id with prerequisites d creates edges d -> id; a cycle appears exactly when some d already depends on id transitively.
Search from id along existing dependents (tasks that listed id) and reject if a prerequisite of the new task is reached.
For the order, run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap; tasks waiting on a missing prerequisite never reach in-degree zero, nor do their dependents.
invariants: the stored graph is always acyclic
the returned order lists a task only after all its prerequisites
chooseWhen: Build systems and schedulers that accept tasks over time
tradeoffs: Per-add cycle checks can cost O(V) each; batching additions and checking once is cheaper when rejection details are not needed
hack2hire:68a61ebd3a368733bb10424d.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: incremental DAG with cycle rejection and smallest-id order

constraints: filterName is one of even, odd, positive, negative, nonzero
up to 2e5 calls; next only when an element remains
clarifyingQuestions: How is the filter passed: a function, a predicate object or a name?
What should next() do when nothing is left?
Should elements be filtered eagerly or lazily?
May the iterator copy or modify the list?
hints: Keep a cursor into the list instead of copying it.
hasNext skips elements the predicate rejects and stops at the next accepted one without consuming it.
next calls hasNext first, then returns the element at the cursor and advances past it.
invariants: the cursor never moves backwards
every returned element satisfies the predicate
chooseWhen: Streaming filters over large or lazy sources
tradeoffs: A lazy cursor keeps O(1) memory but repeats predicate work if hasNext is called many times without caching
hack2hire:678dc780fa7ce9616e190fb7.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: lazy filtering iterator with named predicates

clarifyingQuestions: How far does a jump go?
How does currentHeight change after landing?
When does the walk end, and what is returned?
What if the walk never ends?
hints: After the first jump the height always equals nums at the current position, so the state is just (position, direction).
There are only 2n states; a repeated state means the walk loops forever.
Record states in a hash set (or a 2n-entry visited array) and stop at the first repeat or the first jump that leaves the array.
invariants: the state (position, direction) determines the rest of the walk
the walk makes at most 2n successful jumps before a state repeats
chooseWhen: Deterministic walks that may cycle
tradeoffs: A visited array is faster than a hash set but costs 2n entries even for short walks
hack2hire:6a14d69a7b0582b352787fa8.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: alternating jumps of the current height

constraints: set only for absent keys, update only for present keys
clarifyingQuestions: What does prefix search return: keys, values or pairs, and in which order?
How are the error cases reported?
Does the empty prefix match everything?
Should deleted keys leave trie nodes behind?
hints: A hash map answers get, set, update and delete; a trie answers prefix questions.
Store a live-key count in every trie node so empty branches can be pruned on delete.
Visit children in letter order with an explicit stack to produce values in key order.
invariants: every trie node on a live key's path has a positive count
the hash map and the trie hold the same key set
chooseWhen: Autocomplete-style lookups over a mutable key set
tradeoffs: The trie duplicates keys already in the hash map; a sorted array is smaller but makes inserts O(n)
hack2hire:68099e1fcbb5948f87732b56.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: key-value store with ordered prefix search

constraints: the number of results is at most 2e5
clarifyingQuestions: Which letter does a run of presses produce, and can a group be longer than the letter list?
Are separate presses of the same digit allowed inside a run?
In which order should results be returned?
What is the answer for an empty input?
hints: Only runs of the same digit interact; each run is cut into groups of size 1 to the letter count.
Backtrack over the string: at position i choose a group size g while the next g characters are the same digit.
Trying smaller groups first emits smaller letters first, so the output is already in lexicographic order.
invariants: a group never crosses a change of digit
two different groupings never give the same string
chooseWhen: Enumerating all decodings of a run-length style code
tradeoffs: The output can be exponential in the input length, so bounds on the result size matter more than time per result
hack2hire:67e3915487527b3f41af78b6.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: multi-press keypad decodings

clarifyingQuestions: How are the trees given?
Can values repeat inside one tree?
What if -1 itself is the common value?
Is recursion depth a concern for skewed trees?
hints: A reverse in-order traversal visits a BST from largest to smallest.
Walk both trees downwards at once: when the current values differ, advance the tree with the larger one.
Use explicit stacks so a 1e5-deep skewed tree does not overflow the call stack.
invariants: both cursors only move to smaller values
no common value larger than both current values exists
chooseWhen: Merging sorted sequences stored as trees
tradeoffs: The two-cursor walk needs only O(h) stack, but decoding the level-order input already costs O(n)
hack2hire:67709b6d366afdc1233e4ffc.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: largest shared value of two BSTs

constraints: no self-pair, no repeated pair, no cycle
clarifyingQuestions: What are the conditions on the relationships: a tree, a forest, bounded degree?
Do people with no connections count?
Is the size enough or must the group be listed?
hints: On a forest each component can be solved independently from any root.
For a vertex v, take(v) = 1 + sum of skip(child) and skip(v) = sum of max(take(child), skip(child)).
Process vertices in reverse depth-first order with an explicit stack to avoid recursion limits.
invariants: take(v) never includes two adjacent people
children are finished before their parent
chooseWhen: Independent-set questions on trees
tradeoffs: The DP relies on the forest structure; the general graph problem needs exponential search
hack2hire:69ae2fec4b133b6a8f3a7345.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum independent set in a forest

clarifyingQuestions: In which order should the k elements be listed?
Do equal values count separately?
What if k > w?
hints: Each slide changes the window by one element in and one out.
A sorted copy of the window turns "k largest" into reading its last k slots.
Binary search finds where to insert the new element and where the leaving value sits.
invariants: the maintained array is the current window in ascending order
each output list is non-increasing
chooseWhen: Repeated order-statistic queries on a moving window
tradeoffs: Array insertion moves O(w) items per step; balanced trees or heaps give O(log w) at a higher constant
hack2hire:6910e7e971ea59cda5a81ac4.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: top-k per sliding window

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when no rectangle exists?
Must the sides be parallel to the axes?
Do the four corners have to be input points?
How large can coordinates get, and can the area overflow?
hints: An axis-aligned rectangle is two columns sharing the same pair of y values.
Sweep columns by increasing x; for each pair (y1, y2) the widest rectangle uses the first column where the pair appeared.
Track the best (x - firstX) * (y2 - y1).
invariants: firstX of a pair never changes once set
every scored rectangle has four input corners
chooseWhen: Rectangle detection on lattice points
tradeoffs: The column-pair map can hold O(n^2) entries when columns are tall

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when no rectangle exists?
Must the sides be parallel to the axes?
Do the four corners have to be input points?
How large can coordinates get, and can the area overflow?
hints: A quadrilateral is a rectangle exactly when its diagonals share a midpoint and a length.
Group point pairs by (x1 + x2, y1 + y2, squared distance); any two pairs in a group are the diagonals of a rectangle.
With diagonal (p1, p2) and other corners a, b, the area is |(a - p1) x (b - p1)|, an exact integer.
invariants: pairs in a group share midpoint and length
areas are computed with integers only
chooseWhen: Geometry over lattice points where exact integer arithmetic is possible
tradeoffs: Grouping by exact integer keys avoids floating-point error but can store O(n^2) pairs
hack2hire:69b62ed7666464810ca36212.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: largest rectangle in any orientation
